Mirʾāt al-Zamān remains in manuscript. A complete copy is held in the Feyzullah Efendi Library in Istanbul. I arrived in that great Islamic capital after fleeing Lebanon, where Saudi intelligence had been pursuing me after abducting my companion Nasser al-Saeed. I began consulting the manuscript of Mirʾāt al-Zamān in that library. Before I could finish its first volume, I was approached by a double Saudi-Iraqi intelligence agent. I fled the library and left the next day, returning to Syria. What I quote here from Mirʾāt al-Zamān therefore depends on Abd al-Rahman Badawi’s Sufi Ecstatic Utterances, cited in the text, p. 214; he took it from the Paris manuscript.↩︎

Al-Hallaj’s condemned Tawasin has survived, while al-Junayd’s book opposing al-Hallaj has not. The two men belonged to the same generation. This is one piece of evidence that the loss of Islamic books did not follow a systematic distinction between approved and rejected doctrines; much of it was simply accidental. Among those accidents were burnings of books by Turkish powers, beginning with the Seljuks and the Turks of the later Abbasid age; by the Byzantines during their occupations of parts of Syria and Mosul; and by the Spaniards. Many different kinds of books disappeared in these burnings, approved and disapproved alike. More works of jurisprudence and literature were lost than works of philosophy.↩︎
